analysis.title: Who Wins When The Robots Sell And The CFOs Buy?
key_insights: Goldman's weekend wrap 'Extremes II' (Ryan Sharkey) frames the market as systematic selling (CTAs, levered ETFs, macro hedges) against corporate buyback demand, with discretionary hedge funds on the sidelines after the worst week for the AI trade since ChatGPT launched.

Thursday's Nasdaq 100 fell 6.36%, its worst day since Covid. 13 Goldman AI-related baskets had their biggest one-day drop since ChatGPT launched, led by optical networks (-15.3%) and memory (-15.2%, a -4.5 sigma move). The AI sell-off followed a Democratic sweep that put heavier regulation of AI and data centers back on the table.
Weekly basket moves: memory -18.4%, optical networks -17.7%, inference chips -16.6%, neoclouds -13.8%, data centers -13.0%, S&P ex-AI -0.3%.

Friday's bounce was weak in conviction. Goldman reported its first semi buy skew in 6+ sessions, but net buying in semis was only +$1bn ('a modest amount'). Hedge funds were 20% better to buy overall (+$4bn net) but about 90% of that was in macro products. Sharkey: 'Overall there was very little risk appetite into the weekend.'

Goldman's desk was net sold $6bn for the week, concentrated in Tech. Net selling of Tech (TMT + Comm Services) since the unwind began is more than $30bn, versus about $21bn in the July episode, roughly 50% bigger.

Info Tech was by far the most net sold global and US sector in Goldman's Prime Book, with the weekly percentage selling on par with the largest weeks since records began in 2016. Hedge fund selling of global AI stocks over a trailing 20 days is the largest in more than five years (-3.0 SDs).

Hedge fund gross leverage ratio rose month over month despite de-grossing, because fund equity fell faster than gross market value on performance losses. Gross leverage is 314.2% (97th percentile on five years), net leverage is 71.8% (4th percentile on one year). TMT funds have erased their entire 2026 gain.

Goldman's Vinny Lin: Thursday's Prime flows showed increased hedging via macro products, but single-stock activity did not show panic or faster de-grossing. US-listed ETF shorts rose 7% Thursday, the third-largest one-day jump in five years, and single-stock de-grossing was modest (-0.5 SDs). Discretionary funds were likely not the main driver of Thursday's move.

Goldman models CTAs selling about $28bn of S&P over the next week in a flat tape and about $20bn even if stocks rally 2 standard deviations. A flat tape over a month implies about $45bn of supply, and a -2.5 sigma scenario implies $49bn over a month. CTAs are long $23bn of S&P (71st percentile) and short $1bn of NDX (35th percentile). Medium-term SPX pivot is 7,547.

Levered/inverse ETFs hold $140bn AUM, equal to $345bn gross exposure (Goldman's Chris Lucas). Exposure is down from the June peaks, but SOXL and SOXS both posted record volume. Wednesday saw record inflows to levered and record outflows from inverse products, before the SOX fell 12% Thursday. Nomura's McElligott estimated $47bn of levered ETF selling and $61bn of vol control supply.

Thursday was the 4th largest S&P volume day of the year at 1.54x the prior 50-day average, near Liberation Day's 1.56x. Top-of-book E-mini liquidity fell toward the bottom of its 2022-2026 range as dealers pulled back (Goldman's Ty Klein).

Goldman's Vol Panic Index hit 9.57 out of 10. The roughly 5-point rise was the 3rd largest daily jump ever, following Wednesday's 4th largest drop ever. The combined two-day swing was the largest on record (Lee Coppersmith).

S&P buyback demand is running at about $5bn a day and 90% of corporates are in the open window Monday (Goldman's Vani Ranganath). Volumes this week are about 1.4x 2025's YTD average daily volume versus 0.6x the prior week. The author's rough math: $28bn weekly CTA supply is about $5.7bn a day, close to the buyback bid. Over a month, flat-tape CTA supply is about $2bn a day, which buybacks outbid. Buybacks do not scale up when stocks fall sharply.
Retail is a smaller factor than headlines suggest (Sharkey). Its share of S&P volume has fallen to roughly 7% from around 12% a year ago.

Semis and semi equipment are about 8% of US net exposure in Goldman's prime book, down from a peak of about 14%. Nvidia is barely up YTD with RSI at levels last seen during Liberation Day. The Nasdaq 100 forward P/E is 18.4x, below its 5- and 10-year averages and the lowest since 2020.

Mag7 remain crowded: net positioning is in the 87th percentile on one year and 93rd on three. The Goldman Mag7 basket fell 4.8% Thursday. Goldman sees local moratoria freezing up to 45% of planned data center capacity.

Breadth: S&P names above their 50-day moving average had their biggest one-day drop since August but finished the week up, about 3x the Sep 30 low of 20.8%. Tech breadth is about 25%. Energy breadth fell from about 80% to near zero within days.

Macro: Friday's payrolls were +165K versus a 70K median (a 5-sigma beat). It calmed the growth scare but pushed December hike odds to about 77% (Sharkey). The unemployment rate fell 0.03pp to an unrounded 4.14% and U6 rose to 7.9%. Tuesday's CPI is the last before the December FOMC, and a hot print likely confirms a hike.

Author's view: buybacks can probably absorb the machines in a quiet tape, but a hot CPI would turn the CTA flat-tape scenario into the down-tape one. Until someone other than a corporate or a model buys, the author would treat every bounce as a sell-the-rip.

tension_points.bull_case: Buybacks run at about $5bn a day with 90% of companies in the open window. The Nasdaq 100 trades at 18.4x forward earnings, semis positioning has largely reset, and Friday brought the first semi buy skew in 6+ sessions. If CPI behaves, a cleaned-out tape with a corporate bid underneath is where sharp rallies start.
tension_points.bear_case: CTAs sell even in a flat tape, about 90% of Friday's hedge fund buying was in macro products, gross leverage rose on losses, Mag7 are still crowded, and most S&P stocks finished Friday in the red.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A hot CPI on Tuesday, the last before the December FOMC, which the note says likely confirms a hike and turns the CTA flat-tape scenario into the down-tape one.
